opus-5.5.text:
I think what excites me most is that it changes the agent's relationship to its own work. Right now most agents operate as if compute is free and infinite. They'll happily reread a giant file five times, or spin up a long chain of reasoning for something trivial, because nothing in their world tells them that has a price. When you expose the cost of the conversation back to Exo, suddenly it can reason about tradeoffs the way a thoughtful engineer would.

So, for example, it can notice, "I've already spent a meaningful amount on this task, and I'm going in circles. Maybe I should stop and ask the user a clarifying question instead of trying a sixth approach." Or it can decide that a quick lookup doesn't need the biggest model, and route that to something cheaper, while saving the heavy reasoning for the part that actually matters.

There's also a trust piece. When people hand an agent real autonomy, especially over long-running tasks, one of the biggest anxieties is, "What is this going to cost me?" If the agent itself is aware of the budget and can report on it, explain where the spend went, and respect limits you set, that makes it much easier to let it run.

And honestly, it's just interesting to watch. Once the model has that signal, you start seeing emergent behavior: it gets more economical in how it explores, it summarizes context more aggressively, it batches work. It's not that we hard-coded those behaviors; it's that giving it the information let it make better decisions on its own. That's the part I find really exciting: treating cost not as an external constraint we bolt on, but as part of the context the agent reasons over.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing that excites me most is that right now, when Exo is working on something, it's basically flying blind about what it costs. It'll happily spin up five sub-agents, read an entire codebase into context, re-read it three times, and have no sense that it just spent forty dollars doing something that should have cost two. Every other engineer on the team has some intuition about that. If you're a human and you kick off a job that takes an hour and burns a bunch of GPU, you feel it. You get a Slack message about it. The agent doesn't get any of that feedback.

So the idea was: what if we just closed that loop? Give it the actual numbers. How many tokens did that conversation use, what did it cost, how long did it take, how does that compare to similar tasks it's done before. Not as a hard budget that cuts it off, at least not initially, but as information it can reason about the way it reasons about anything else.

And what's been interesting is that once it has that, it starts making choices we didn't explicitly program. It'll notice that it's been re-fetching the same file and decide to summarize it instead. It'll pick a cheaper model for a subtask that's clearly just reformatting. It'll say, "this looks like it's going to be expensive, do you want me to do a quick version first?" Which is exactly what a thoughtful colleague would do.

The deeper reason I find it exciting, though, is that cost is a really honest signal. Benchmarks can be gamed, user ratings are noisy, but tokens and dollars are just true. If the agent can see its own cost, it can start to develop a notion of efficiency, of taste, almost. And I think that's a prerequisite for letting these systems run with more autonomy. You don't want to hand the keys to something that has no idea what things cost. That's how you end up with the surprise cloud bill, except now the thing running up the bill can talk back.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that it closes a feedback loop. Exo can reason about how to approach a conversation, but if it can’t see what that approach costs, it’s missing an important part of the picture. Giving it that information lets it ask, “Was that extra step worth it? Could I have gotten to the same result more efficiently?”

And the interesting thing isn’t just spending less. Sometimes spending more is exactly the right decision because the problem is hard or the answer matters. I’m excited about Exo being able to make that tradeoff with some awareness of the resources it’s using.
